845: Well now, a rare visitor. You’re the one in the attic with the plants on the sill, aren’t you? Bà Lan told me about you.
846: My eyes aren’t what they were, and these shelves have got all jumbled. Would you help me sort one? Just by colour, so it’s nice to look at.
847: At my shop, anyone who helps tidy a shelf gets to borrow a book. My late wife made that rule years ago.
848: That’s my wife’s handwriting. She had a habit of pressing flowers in books. Every book she finished, she left one inside.
849: I thought I’d put them all away, but it seems one was still on the shelf. Would you keep this daisy for me a few more days? I’m not quite brave enough to look at it for long.
850: Would you read a page aloud for me? It doesn’t have to be good. Just read slowly. It’s been a long time since this shop heard someone reading.
851: My wife loved that line too. The two of you would have got along.
852: Before I put the book back on the shelf, would you like to tuck something inside?
853: You press flowers too? I thought that sweet little habit had left with her. I’ve had an idea: I’ll keep a shelf just for “Books with Flowers”. Anyone who borrows one can tuck a flower back in. A little more spring for the shop.
854: No pressed flowers yet? That’s all right. When your plants up there bloom, press one and bring it down. I’ll keep this book at the counter for you.
855: I’ve kept this tucked in a drawer for a long time. It’s my wife’s pressed-flower album, and there are still a few blank pages at the back. I think you’ll fill them in far more beautifully than I ever could. Your library card is full of stamps now too, so here’s a gold one. Borrow as long as you like.
856: My late wife’s rule: tidy a shelf, borrow a book. Help me sort one today first, would you?
857: This shelf looks so much happier now. Thank you. My eyes just got one shelf brighter, thanks to you.
858: Red, orange, yellow, green… like a rainbow napping on the shelf. My wife would have said you have clever hands.
859: Done already? Much faster than I ever was. When I was young I sorted by author, and she liked sorting by colour. We argued about it for years.
860: The shelf is tidy for today. Come back tomorrow and help with another. The dust in this shop never runs out.
861: I saved this one for you. Just one page a day. Old books are like old people, they don’t like to be rushed.
862: How far along are you in the book you borrowed? Take your time. Bring it back once you’ve read the last page.
863: Back right on time, and the pages still smooth. You’re my favourite reader in the whole shop.
864: How did you find this one? Tell me about it next time. I love hearing young people talk about books.
865: My wife and I opened this shop when we were young. Back then the lane had no bougainvillea, just one dim yellow streetlamp.
866: I’ve worn these reading glasses for ten years. Now they and I are equally blurry, ha ha.
867: Don’t worry about creasing the pages. Books get their creases from being read, like faces get their wrinkles from smiling.
868: Rainy days are quiet in the shop, but I like them. Rain on the tin roof and one good chapter. That’s an afternoon well spent.
869: You have the gold card now, so pick whichever book you like. Tell me about it when you’re done.
870: Mr. Khải runs the old bookshop at the end of the lane, and he could use a helping hand these days. If you have time, drop by. He’d be so glad.
871: Rainy Season in the Old Town
872: That rainy season, the old town had a little tea shop tucked under an awning. People stepped in to wait out the rain, and stayed longer than they meant to.
873: The owner never asked what anyone wanted to drink. She looked at them for a moment, then poured exactly the tea they needed.
874: At the end of the season, she only said: “Every rain stops in the end. All we need is a warm place to wait.”
876: Some letters are written and then put away in a drawer. Not because we don’t want to send them, but because writing them was enough.
877: The retired old postman still walked through the old lanes every day, greeting each mailbox like an old friend.
878: He said: “It’s all right if a letter arrives a little late. As long as someone is still waiting for it.”
880: On the roof of an old apartment block, someone grew a whole garden in paint buckets. Tomatoes, herbs, a few clumps of daisies.
881: Each neighbour gave a little: some brought seeds, some brought soil, some just came up to water while the gardener was away.
882: When the flowers bloomed, the whole block climbed up to watch the sunset. No one remembered who had started the garden anymore.
884: In a seaside town lived an old lighthouse keeper. Every evening he climbed the tower, wiped the glass and lit the lamp.
885: Some years no ships passed by at all, and still he lit it. He said a light isn’t only for showing the way. It’s also so someone knows they’re not alone.
886: When he could no longer climb the stairs, the town’s children took turns lighting it. The lamp has not gone dark a single night.
888: The little girl had a yellow umbrella, and she carried it even on sunny days.
889: When people asked, she said: “In case someone forgets theirs, we can share.”
890: Only when she grew up did she understand: that umbrella sheltered her far more than she ever sheltered anyone else.
892: A young man drew a map with no roads, only little things: the place with the best-smelling bánh mì, the step that catches the morning sun, the tree where a cat sleeps.
893: Whenever he felt sad, he opened the map and went to just one of those places.
894: He said the map didn’t help him go further. It helped him remember where he was.
895: That morning, she opened the shop earlier than usual.
896: The sun wasn’t fully up yet. There was only the smell of old paper and sparrows chirping out on the porch.
897: She laid a daisy between the pages and closed the book so gently, as if afraid to startle the flower.
898: Some things only need to be kept, not said.
899: A pressed flower is no longer fresh, but the spring is still inside it.
900: One page read slowly is worth more than ten pages read in a hurry.
